title: X. “It Was He Who Said That”
paragraphs: Alyosha, as soon as he arrived, told Ivan that a little more than an hour before, Marya Kondratyevna had come running to his rooms with the news that Smerdyakov had killed himself. “I went in to clear away the samovar, and there he was, hanging from a nail in the wall.” Alyosha had asked whether she had told the police. She said she had told nobody, “but I flew straight to you, I ran the whole way.” She seemed to Alyosha completely out of her mind, and she was shaking like a leaf. He had run with her to the cottage and found Smerdyakov still hanging there. On the table was a note: “I destroy my life of my own will and desire, so as to put no blame on anyone.” Alyosha had left the note where it lay, gone straight to the police captain and told him the whole story. “And from him I’ve come straight to you,” Alyosha concluded, looking hard into Ivan’s face. All through his account he had kept his eyes on Ivan, as though something in his expression had startled him.
“Brother,” he cried suddenly, “you must be terribly ill. You look at me, and you don’t seem to take in what I’m telling you.”
“I’m glad you came,” said Ivan, as if he were brooding, and he did not hear Alyosha’s outcry. “I knew he had hanged himself.”
“Who told you?”
“I don’t know. But I knew. Did I know? Yes, he told me. He told me just now.”
Ivan stood in the middle of the room and kept on speaking in the same brooding tone, with his eyes on the floor.
“Who is _he_?” asked Alyosha, looking round the room before he could stop himself.
“He’s slipped away.”
Ivan lifted his head and gave a faint smile.

“He was afraid of you, of a dove like you. You’re a ‘pure cherub.’ Dmitri calls you a cherub. Cherub!... the thunderous rapture of the seraphim. What are seraphim? Perhaps a whole constellation. Or perhaps that constellation is nothing but a chemical molecule. There’s a constellation called the Lion and the Sun. Don’t you know it?”
“Brother, sit down,” said Alyosha, alarmed. “Please, sit down on the sofa! You’re delirious. Lay your head on the pillow, yes, like that. Would you like a wet towel for your forehead? It might help.”
“Give me the towel. It’s on the chair there. I just threw it down.”

“It isn’t there. Don’t trouble yourself. I know where it is—here,” said Alyosha. In the far corner, by Ivan’s dressing-table, he had found a clean towel, still folded and never used. Ivan stared at the towel oddly, and for an instant his memory seemed to return.

“Wait”—he rose from the sofa—“an hour ago I took that new towel from over there and soaked it. I wrapped it around my head and then threw it down here ... How can it be dry? There wasn’t another one.”
“You put that towel on your head?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, and I paced up and down the room with it an hour ago ... Why have the candles burned so low? What time is it?”
“Nearly twelve.”

“No, no, no!” Ivan cried suddenly. “It was not a dream. He was here. He sat right here, on that sofa. When you knocked on the window, I threw a glass at him ... this one. Wait a minute. The last time I really was asleep, but this dream was no dream. It’s happened before. I have dreams now, Alyosha ... but they’re not dreams, they’re real. I walk about, I talk, I see ... and all the while I’m asleep. But he was sitting here, on that sofa over there.... He’s frightfully stupid, Alyosha, frightfully stupid.” Ivan gave a sudden laugh and started pacing the room.
“Who is stupid? Who do you mean, brother?” Alyosha asked once more, anxiously.

“The devil! He’s taken to visiting me. He’s been here twice, nearly three times. He taunted me for being angry that he is only a plain devil and not Satan, with singed wings, amid thunder and lightning. But he isn’t Satan. That’s a lie. He’s a fraud. He’s simply a devil—a paltry, petty devil. He goes to the baths. Undress him and you’ll certainly find a tail, long and smooth like a Great Dane’s, a yard long, dun-colored.... Alyosha, you’re freezing. You’ve been out in the snow. Would you like some tea? What? Is it cold? Shall I tell her to bring some? _C’est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors._...”
Alyosha ran to the washstand, soaked the towel, coaxed Ivan into sitting down again and wound the wet towel around his head. Then he sat down next to him.

“What was it you told me just now about Lise?” Ivan began again. (He was becoming very talkative.) “I like Lise. I said something nasty about her, and it was a lie. I like her ... I’m afraid of Katya tomorrow. I’m more afraid of her than of anything else, because of the future. Tomorrow she’ll cast me off and trample me underfoot. She thinks I’m destroying Mitya out of jealousy over her! Yes, that’s what she thinks! But it’s not so. Tomorrow the cross, but not the gallows. No, I won’t hang myself. Do you know, I could never commit suicide, Alyosha. Is that because I’m base? I’m no coward. Is it love of life? How did I know that Smerdyakov had hanged himself? Yes, _he_ told me.”
“And you’re completely certain that someone has been here?” asked Alyosha.

“Yes, on that sofa in the corner. You would have driven him off. You did drive him off: he vanished when you came in. I love your face, Alyosha. Did you know that I loved your face? And _he_ is myself, Alyosha. All that is base in me, all that is mean and contemptible. Yes, I’m a romantic. He guessed that ... though it’s a libel. He’s frightfully stupid, but that serves him well. He has cunning, an animal’s cunning—he knew how to drive me wild. He kept jeering that I believed in him, and that’s how he got me to listen. He fooled me like a boy. But he told me a great deal about myself that was true. I’d never have owned up to it. Do you know, Alyosha,” Ivan added in an intensely earnest, confiding tone, “I’d be awfully glad to think it was _he_ and not I.”
“He has worn you out,” said Alyosha, looking at his brother with pity.

“He’s been teasing me. And he does it so cleverly, you know, so cleverly. ‘Conscience! What is conscience? I make it up myself. Why does it torment me? Out of habit. The habit of all mankind for seven thousand years. So let’s give it up, and we’ll be gods.’ He said that, he said that!”

“And not you, not you?” Alyosha could not help crying out, looking his brother full in the face. “Forget him, in any case. Be rid of him and put him out of your mind. And let him take away everything you curse now, and never return!”

“Yes, but he’s spiteful. He laughed at me. He was insolent, Alyosha,” said Ivan, with a shudder of offense. “But he was unfair to me, unfair to me about lots of things. He told lies about me to my face. ‘Oh, you’re about to perform an act of heroic virtue: you’ll confess that you murdered your father, that the valet killed him at your instigation.’”
“Brother,” Alyosha broke in, “control yourself. You did not murder him. It isn’t true!”

“That’s what he says, he does, and he knows it. ‘You’re about to perform an act of heroic virtue, and you don’t believe in virtue. That’s what torments you and makes you furious, that’s why you’re so vengeful.’ He said that to me about me, and he knows what he’s saying.”
“It’s you saying that, not he,” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, “and you say it because you’re sick and feverish and torturing yourself.”

“No, he knows what he’s saying. ‘You’re going out of pride,’ he says. ‘You’ll stand up and say, I killed him, so why do you squirm with horror? You’re lying! I despise your opinion, I despise your horror!’ He said that about me. ‘And do you know that you’re longing for their praise—“he is a criminal, a murderer, but what a noble soul; he wanted to save his brother and so he confessed.”’ That’s a lie, Alyosha!” Ivan cried suddenly, his eyes flashing. “I don’t want the low rabble praising me, I swear I don’t! It’s a lie! That’s why I threw the glass at him, and it smashed against his ugly face.”
“Brother, calm down, stop!” Alyosha begged him.

“Yes, he knows how to torture a man. He’s cruel,” Ivan went on, paying no attention. “From the very first I had a suspicion of what he’d come for. ‘Suppose you’re going out of pride, still you hoped that Smerdyakov would be convicted and sent to Siberia, and Mitya would be acquitted, and you would get off with nothing worse than moral condemnation’ (‘Do you hear?’ he laughed at that point)—‘and some people would praise you. But now Smerdyakov is dead, he has hanged himself, and who will believe you, one man alone? And yet you’re going, you’re going, you’ll go all the same, you’ve made up your mind to go. So what are you going for now?’ It’s dreadful, Alyosha. I can’t bear questions like that. Who dares to ask me such questions?”

“Brother,” Alyosha put in—his heart sank in terror, but he still seemed to hope he could bring Ivan back to his senses—“how could he have told you of Smerdyakov’s death before I came, when nobody knew about it and nobody had had time to?”

“He told me,” said Ivan firmly, refusing to allow a doubt. “It was all he talked about, if you want to know. ‘It would be all right if you believed in virtue,’ he said. ‘It wouldn’t matter if they didn’t believe you, you’d be going on principle. But you’re a little pig like Fyodor Pavlovitch, so what do you want with virtue? Why do you want to go meddling, if your sacrifice does nobody any good? Because you yourself don’t know why you’re going! Oh, you’d give a great deal to know why you’re going! And have you actually made up your mind? You haven’t. You’ll sit up all night debating whether to go or not. But you will go. You know you will. You know that whichever way you decide, the decision doesn’t rest with you. You’ll go because you won’t dare not to go. Why won’t you dare? Guess that for yourself. That’s a riddle for you!’ Then he got up and left. You arrived and he went. He called me a coward, Alyosha! _Le mot de l’énigme_ is that I’m a coward. ‘It is not for such eagles to soar above the earth.’ He was the one who added that—he! And Smerdyakov said the same thing. He must be killed! Katya despises me. I’ve seen it for a month now. Even Lise will start to despise me! ‘You’re going in order to be praised.’ What a brutal lie! And you despise me too, Alyosha. Now I’m going to hate you again! And I hate the monster, too! I hate the monster! I don’t want to save the monster. Let him rot in Siberia! He’s started singing a hymn! Oh, tomorrow I’ll go, I’ll stand in front of them and spit in their faces!”

He leaped up in a frenzy, tore off the towel, and began pacing the room again. Alyosha remembered what Ivan had said a little earlier: “I seem to be sleeping awake.... I walk, I speak, I see, but I am asleep.” That was exactly how it looked now. Alyosha stayed with him. The thought crossed his mind of running for a doctor, but he was afraid to leave his brother alone, and he had no one to leave him with. Gradually Ivan lost consciousness altogether. He kept talking, talking without pause, but quite incoherently, and he could barely form his words. All at once he lurched violently, but Alyosha caught him in time. Ivan let himself be led to his bed. Somehow Alyosha got his clothes off and put him to bed. He sat and watched over him for another two hours. The sick man slept deeply, without moving, breathing softly and evenly. Alyosha took a pillow and lay down on the sofa in his clothes.

As he fell asleep he prayed for Mitya and for Ivan. He was beginning to understand Ivan’s illness. “The anguish of a proud resolve. A serious conscience!” God, in Whom he did not believe, and God’s truth were winning mastery over his heart, which still refused to give way. “Yes,” the thought drifted through Alyosha’s head as it lay on the pillow, “yes, if Smerdyakov is dead, no one will believe Ivan’s testimony, but he will go and give it.” Alyosha smiled gently. “God will conquer!” he thought. “Either Ivan will rise into the light of truth, or ... he will perish in hatred, taking revenge on himself and on everyone for having served a cause he does not believe in,” Alyosha added bitterly, and again he prayed for Ivan.
